project.title: Glove, Visor, Rover
project.description: A speculative probe rover for gloved salvage workers on Proxima b: a glove squeeze, one hand and the voice steer it, and fixed rules overrule a local language model.
project.introText: A salvage worker in a sealed suit and thick gloves, his hands on a tool and his radio busy with the team, sends Junior, a probe rover, ahead with a squeeze, one hand and his voice, so he never has to walk up to a hazard himself. The setting is Proxima b as we imagined it: earlier inhabitants marked buried hazards in infrared that humans cannot see, and a fungus glows over them.

gridImages.caption: Our midterm started from nuclear semiotics: warnings that must still work long after anyone can read them, the premise of the whole world.
The world we wrote for it: settlers on Proxima b dug into sealed sites whose warnings were written in light they cannot see.
We grounded the world in signals already present today, from repository disputes to gesture-controlled gloves, so the fiction stays tied to real debates.
The science under the fiction: the builders marked danger in light we cannot see, and a glowing fungus became the warning we can read.
Marvin, the salvage worker we wrote, and the suit's channels, each chosen for a sealed suit, busy hands and orange light.
The suit as one sealed object, built in layers, drawing on diving suits, firefighter gear and hazmat suits.
Our initial prototype, built on the lab examples: a first glow detector and visor, and the open question of whether stated certainty gets over-trusted.
The final starts with the Arduino car, in a frame from a voice test: one of Junior's two parts, steered by gestures and speech.
The suit narrowed to a glove and a rover; each input gets one role, and the fixed rules never wait for the model.
The palm switch makes the squeeze a gate that says only “now”, with thresholds that ignore a brush and stop Junior on every switch.
One-hand gestures, kept coarse so a work glove can make them and the other hand stays free, each echoed back on the visor.
Cloned voices let Junior answer each of us in our own voice, and the response times show why only fixed rules handle “stop”.
The second part: the 3D Junior, which runs the whole system, taking Marvin's shift from the first squeeze to the way home.
The autopilot replaced retracing every step with a straight way home, and an open hand can always take control back from it.
Glove tests with classmates and our logged response times measure how legible the inputs are, not yet what Marvin would experience.
What holds up, what each part runs, what comes next, and the question we end on: a confident Junior in a voice Marvin trusts.
All sources from both presentations in one list, with a note on how every picture on these plates was made.

project.middleText: What held up: every camera switch stops Junior first, and a work glove barely changed the gesture scores. Still open: a test with people who work in gloves rather than classmates, a wireless glove, a way home without drift, and consent for cloned voices.
project.highlightCaption: From the final demo: the 3D Junior on its home ring, with fungus glowing over buried hazards. Our own code drives it: Junior's brain, the visor and glow detection.
project.context: Multimodal Interaction Design, MSc Information Studies, University of Amsterdam

summary.brief: Salvage workers on Proxima b dig in sealed suits and thick gloves among hazards marked in infrared they cannot see, and checking a site means walking up to it.
summary.role: A group project, in a team of four.
summary.method: A speculative world built on published research, a persona, weekly prototypes from a gesture car to the 3D Junior, and tests of the squeeze and gestures with three testers, plus logged response times.
summary.outcome: A prototype in two parts: the Arduino car, a two-hand gesture car that also takes voice commands, and the 3D Junior, which runs the whole system with one-hand gestures; a browser version is on this page.
summary.stack: Arduino, Python, MediaPipe, Whisper, Gemma 3 4B (Ollama), XTTS v2, force-sensitive resistor

facts: median for a fixed-rule command such as “stop” (15 logged); speech recognition alone 0.25 s
hard presses switched the camera; a natural grip did once in 40 (three testers)

project.shows: Multimodal input designed as relations between channels, with fixed limits on what a language model may decide, prototyped on a physical car and in a 3D world.

decisions.choice: Narrow the whole suit to one rover and one glove.
decisions.why: At the midterm the TAs said a whole suit “might be a lot”, and a rover keeps the worker away from the hazard: Junior goes up to it in his place.
decisions.result: Hand, voice and squeeze each got a prototype of their own, week by week, before they were joined in the 3D Junior.

decisions.choice: Fixed rules act before the language model, and the model never moves Junior.
decisions.why: A command that goes through Gemma, like “check that one”, takes a median of 2.3 seconds (62 logged commands): too slow for an emergency.
decisions.result: “Stop” works by voice, fist and squeeze, a driving hand cancels the autopilot, and the model only proposes which glow to check.

decisions.choice: Let Junior speak in the cloned voices of the crew.
decisions.why: After Sebeok's 1984 proposal to keep nuclear warnings alive by retelling them: Marvin could hear a warning in the voice of the teammate he lost.
decisions.result: Built with XTTS v2: Junior answers three of us in our own voices, and anyone else in a blend of the three. A voice Marvin trusts also makes over-trust easier (Parasuraman & Riley, 1997).

tryIt.title: Try the 3D Junior
tryIt.intro: The 3D Junior, in your browser: drive it by keyboard or touch, or by hand and voice if you allow your webcam and microphone. Click a glowing patch to point at it; here the fixed rules pick the glow, without the language model.
tryIt.note: About 4 MB, loaded when you press start. Camera and microphone are asked for only if you turn them on.

video.title: The Arduino car
video.caption: A voice test of the Arduino car on 8 October 2026, filmed from above on a floor at home: setting a base, then moving, stopping, turning and reversing the car by voice, and sending it back to base.
